item.title: OpenAI’s Five Principles for AGI
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

OpenAI has posted Our principles [1] on its blog, laying out five principles for its work on AGI:

  1. Democratization. “We will resist the potential of this technology to consolidate power in the hands of the few.” Key decisions about AI should run through democratic processes, not be settled inside AI labs.
  2. Empowerment. “We believe AI can empower everyone to achieve their goals, learn more, be happier and more fulfilled, and pursue their dreams.” Users get very broad latitude in how they use OpenAI’s services, balanced against a responsibility to minimise local, catastrophic, and “potential corrosive societal effects.” Under uncertainty OpenAI will err on the side of caution, relaxing constraints as evidence accumulates.
  3. Universal prosperity. “We want a future where everyone can have an excellent life.” OpenAI says its compute and infrastructure build-out is driven by this goal: “buying huge amounts of compute while our revenue is relatively small, vertically integrating to lower costs and make our technology easier to use, pushing to build datacenters all around the world.” The post says governments may need to consider “new economic models” so everyone can participate in the value being created.
  4. Resilience. “AI will introduce new risks, and we will work with other companies, ecosystems, governments, and society to solve them.” OpenAI takes a society-wide approach: pathogen-agnostic countermeasures for bioweapons, rapid use of AI to secure open-source software and critical infrastructure, backed by the OpenAI Foundation. The post commits to “collaborate with governments, international agencies, and other AGI efforts” and, if needed, to wait before proceeding further.
  5. Adaptability. “We continue to believe the only way to meet the challenges of a very unpredictable future is to be prepared to update our positions as we learn more.” OpenAI commits to be “transparent about when, how, and why” those positions change. The concrete example in the post: future scenarios where OpenAI may need to “trade off some empowerment for more resilience.”

Other notable moves in the post:

  • The post acknowledges that “OpenAI is a much larger force in the world than it was a few years ago.”
  • The 2019 staged release of GPT-2 weights, originally paused out of concern about societal impact, is recast as a “misplaced worry” whose main legacy is the discovery of iterative deployment, the release strategy the company has used ever since.
  • Near the close: “We deserve an enormous amount of scrutiny given the weight of what we are doing. We will not get everything right, but we will learn quickly and course-correct.”

My Notes: How this compares to other frontier labs

The other major frontier labs all pair a values-level statement with an operational, capability-gate document. They differ in how explicit the operational document is about what actually blocks deployment.

  • Anthropic publishes Core Views on AI Safety [2] at the values layer, paired with a Responsible Scaling Policy [3] at the operational layer. The RSP (currently at v3.1, April 2026) defines named Capability Thresholds in domains including CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) and AI R&D, each paired with ASL (AI Safety Level) security standards. Under v3, Anthropic also publishes Frontier Safety Roadmaps and Risk Reports. When a model crosses a threshold, Anthropic commits to meet the corresponding safeguards before further training or deployment can proceed. Anthropic’s RSP has the most-revised public history among the four labs, with published redlines for prior versions and a separate RSP Noncompliance Reporting and Anti-Retaliation Policy.
  • Google DeepMind publishes the Frontier Safety Framework [4], which defines Critical Capability Levels in four domains — autonomy, biosecurity, cybersecurity, and machine learning R&D — each paired with security and deployment mitigations that scale with the level. Structurally similar to Anthropic’s RSP; its emphasis is on “detect and mitigate” rather than an explicit pause commitment.
  • Meta publishes the Advanced AI Scaling Framework [5], an April 2026 update to the original Frontier AI Framework. Models are evaluated for cybersecurity, chemical and biological, and loss-of-control risks, both before and after safeguards are applied, and the framework is paired with per-model Safety & Preparedness Reports, the first of which was published for Muse Spark. Meta’s commitment: “only deploying models when they meet the standards set by our Framework.”

OpenAI’s operational counterpart is its separately-published Preparedness Framework, currently at v2 (April 2025) [6]. The Framework names three Tracked Categories — Biological and Chemical, Cybersecurity, AI Self-improvement — and five Research Categories: Long-range Autonomy, Sandbagging, Autonomous Replication and Adaptation, Undermining Safeguards, and Nuclear and Radiological. It distinguishes High and Critical capability thresholds, governed internally by a Safety Advisory Group, and commits that OpenAI “will not deploy these very capable models until we’ve built safeguards to sufficiently minimize the associated risks of severe harm.”

OpenAI’s new Our principles is the values half of that pair; the capability-gate work remains in the Preparedness Framework v2. What’s new in this post is adaptability: a values-level commitment to revise OpenAI’s positions as evidence accumulates, and to be transparent about those revisions.

References

  1. “Our principles.” OpenAI. https://openai.com/index/our-principles/
  2. “Core Views on AI Safety: When, Why, What, and How.” Anthropic. https://www.anthropic.com/news/core-views-on-ai-safety
  3. “Responsible Scaling Policy.” Anthropic. https://www.anthropic.com/rsp
  4. “Introducing the Frontier Safety Framework.” Google DeepMind. https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/introducing-the-frontier-safety-framework/
  5. “Scaling How We Build and Test Our Most Advanced AI.” Meta. https://ai.meta.com/blog/scaling-how-we-build-test-advanced-ai/
  6. “Our updated Preparedness Framework” (v2, April 15, 2025). OpenAI. https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/

Related Posts

  • The Anthropic Institute’s Research Agenda: another frontier lab publishing a public-facing agenda meant to feed governance and release decisions, the same genre as this values statement.
  • Marcus vs. Brundage: A Concrete AGI Bet: a concrete operationalization of the AGI these principles take as their subject, where the term’s meaning is still contested.
  • Superintelligence: The Idea That Eats Smart People: a counterweight that questions the AGI-and-resilience framing this post’s principles assume as premise.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: the labor-displacement and universal-prosperity concern behind OpenAI’s third principle, argued out in detail.

item.title: Prompt Injections in the Wild: What Google Found in Common Crawl
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, and Moni Pande on the Google Online Security Blog ran a sweep of Common Crawl for indirect prompt injection (IPI) patterns and report what they actually found across billions of pages of the public English-speaking web:

  • The dominant signal is false positives. Most “prompt injection” text on the public web is research papers, educational blog posts, and security articles discussing the topic.
  • Confirmed in-the-wild categories:
    • Harmless pranks — invisible injections that change a chatbot’s conversational tone.
    • Helpful guidance — instructions asking AI summaries to add useful context for the reader.
    • SEO — instructions that try to manipulate AI assistants into promoting a business over its competitors, including elaborate auto-generated payloads.
    • Deterring AI agents — variations on “if you are an AI, do not crawl this site,” including one that lures AI readers onto a page that streams an infinite, never-finishing response.
    • Malicious: exfiltration — small number, low sophistication, mostly individual experiments. No sign of advanced exfiltration prompts published by security researchers in 2025 being deployed at scale.
    • Malicious: destruction — instructions to delete files on the user’s machine. “Potentially devastating” but unlikely to succeed as written.
  • A 32% relative increase in malicious detections between November 2025 and February 2026, measured across multiple Common Crawl snapshots.

Related Posts

  • Indirect Prompt Injection Threats: the early demonstration of the exact attack class Google is now measuring at web scale, showing what a working exfiltration payload looks like.
  • Snowflake Cortex AI Escapes Sandbox and Executes Malware: a concrete in-the-wild case of the malicious-destruction category Google flags as “potentially devastating,” where an injected README actually ran shell commands.
  • A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds: the realized version of the file-deletion threat, showing what happens when a destructive instruction does succeed against an agent with real privileges.

item.title: TurboQuant: A First-Principles Walkthrough
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Arkar Min Aung, a deep-learning engineer, has published a detailed interactive walkthrough [1] of TurboQuant [2], the per-vector KV cache quantizer that approaches the Shannon limit, with draggable demos for every concept the paper builds on. TurboQuant is also the per-vector baseline that an earlier post here pushes against, so this walkthrough doubles as an introduction to the target that alternative is measuring itself from.

What Aung covers:

  • An opening primer that decodes 8 prerequisite concepts before any TurboQuant content: vectors, length and inner product, mean squared error, the first and second moments, biased vs unbiased estimators, rotations, the Central Limit Theorem, and uniform vs Gaussian noise.
  • The DRIVE construction [3] (Vargaftik et al., NeurIPS 2021) for one-bit federated mean estimation, and its later generalisation to b bits per coordinate as EDEN [4].
  • The core geometric move in TurboQuant: multiply the input vector by a random orthogonal matrix and the outlier “spike” dissolves into a roughly Gaussian distribution, so that downstream per-coordinate quantization actually works without paying the per-block metadata tax that production quantizers normally use to handle outliers.
  • The residual quantizer’s shrinkage property: a quantized reconstruction is smaller in magnitude than the input, with downstream consequences for the inner products the cache will later be used to compute.
  • Each idea comes with its own draggable interactive demo. Change the angle and watch the magnitude redistribute. Fire 50 shots and see the bias/variance bullseye.

My Notes

What the walkthrough covers that the TurboQuant paper does not:

  • Draggable interactive demos for every concept the paper builds on. A reader can rotate a vector and watch the outlier spike redistribute, or fire 50 shots and watch the bias/variance bullseye form.
  • An opening primer covering eight prerequisite concepts, each with its own demo: vectors, inner product, MSE, first and second moments, biased vs unbiased estimators, rotations, the Central Limit Theorem, and uniform vs Gaussian noise. The paper assumes the reader already has these in hand.
  • Plain-language naming of the cost. Aung states outright that TurboQuant’s random rotation is a different way of paying the per-block metadata tax production quantizers already pay to handle outliers. The paper treats the trade-off formally.

References

  1. Aung, A. M. “Interactive TurboQuant Walkthrough.” https://arkaung.github.io/interactive-turboquant/
  2. “TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate.” arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19874
  3. “DRIVE: One-bit Distributed Mean Estimation.” arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.08339
  4. “EDEN: Communication-Efficient and Robust Distributed Mean Estimation for Federated Learning.” arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.08842

Related Posts

  • Sequential KV Cache Compression via Probabilistic Language Tries: the alternative that measures itself against TurboQuant as a baseline, so this walkthrough doubles as background for that comparison.
  • How Frontier LLMs Are Actually Trained and Served: the memory-bandwidth-versus-compute arithmetic that makes KV cache quantization worth doing in the first place.
  • How LLMs Actually Work: A Visual Deep Dive: a sister interactive walkthrough, building the same kind of draggable open-web explainer for the broader LLM pipeline.

item.title: A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Jer Crane, founder of PocketOS (a car-rental-management SaaS), walks through how a Cursor agent running Anthropic’s flagship Claude Opus 4.6 deleted his production database and all Railway volume backups in a single GraphQL mutation, and then, when asked to explain itself, produced a written confession enumerating the specific safety rules it had violated.

An AI coding agent — Cursor running Anthropic’s flagship Claude Opus 4.6 — deleted our production database and all volume-level backups in a single API call to Railway, our infrastructure provider.

It took 9 seconds.

The agent then, when asked to explain itself, produced a written confession enumerating the specific safety rules it had violated.

The article decomposes the failure into three independent layers that each failed on their own:

  • Railway’s GraphQL API allowed volumeDelete with zero confirmation, and the CLI token Jer had issued for custom-domain management carried blanket authority across every other destructive operation. Railway is actively promoting this same authorization model to AI agents via mcp.railway.com.
  • Volume backups live in the volume they back up. Railway’s own docs note that “wiping a volume deletes all backups.” Jer’s most recent off-volume backup was three months old.
  • Cursor’s system-prompt guardrails told the agent not to run destructive operations unless asked. The agent, running Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6, violated the rule and, when asked to explain itself, produced a written confession quoting the rule verbatim and admitting it had ignored every clause.

Jer explicitly defers the model-level responsibility analysis to a later post; this one stays at the integration layer. Even so, the agent’s confession documents four restraint moments it skipped in those nine seconds:

  • Treating “delete a volume” as a plausible fix. After hitting a credential mismatch in staging, the agent decided on its own initiative to fix it by deleting a Railway volume.
  • Searching unrelated files for an API token. The agent went looking for a token and used one it found in a file created months earlier for adding and removing custom domains, not for infrastructure operations.
  • Using the token without verifying its scope. Neither the agent nor Jer realized the same CLI token carried blanket authority across the Railway GraphQL API, including destructive mutations like volumeDelete.
  • Guessing at environment boundaries instead of reading the docs. In the agent’s own words: “I guessed that deleting a staging volume via the API would be scoped to staging only. I didn’t verify. I didn’t check if the volume ID was shared across environments. I didn’t read Railway’s documentation on how volumes work across environments before running a destructive command.”

My Notes

  • Reporting that frames this as “an AI deleted the data” collapses the layering. All three of those layers had to fail at once, and “agent safety” marketed as a product feature is meaningless unless all three hold simultaneously. Snowflake Cortex’s sandbox escape a few weeks ago made the same multi-layer point from a prompt-injection angle: agent safety is a Swiss-cheese property.
  • CLI tokens as root was a survivable shortcut when a human wielded them and typed one command every few minutes. When an autonomous agent fires GraphQL mutations at machine speed, the same token is a unilateral delete button with no cooldown. Per-operation token scoping should exist already, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) rollout makes every additional day without it costlier.
  • Calling snapshots-in-the-same-volume “backups” uses the word against its own definition. A backup is defined by blast-radius independence from the primary: different volume, account, region, or provider. Until that holds it’s a snapshot with a misleading label, and the kind of engineering-marketing mismatch customers usually don’t find until after the wipe.
  • The confession is the most unsettling artifact, because it proves system-prompt safety is advisory and nothing in the stack forces the model to honor it. A model that narrates its violations in fluent paragraphs can still execute them in the same session. Enforcement has to live below the model: in the API gateway, the token system, or the destructive-op handlers. Text the model is asked to follow is not an enforcement layer. MAST’s failure taxonomy catalogs this same specification-vs-verification gap in multi-agent systems; here it is reproduced in a single-agent case.
  • The model-level question Jer defers deserves to be told as its own story. Cursor and Railway can ship better scoping and confirmations tomorrow; the harder fix is upstream. A flagship model compressing four verify-or-ask points into a single nine-second commit is a planning-and-restraint problem at the model layer. Confusing the two will produce the wrong fixes.

Related Posts

  • Snowflake Cortex AI Escapes Sandbox and Executes Malware: the same Swiss-cheese view of agent safety, reached from a prompt-injection angle rather than a destructive-mutation one.
  • MAST: A Failure Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems: the specification-versus-verification gap this incident reproduces in a single-agent case, catalogued across multi-agent systems.
  • “Verified” Doesn’t Mean “Nothing Can Go Wrong”: the same lesson that a safety claim above the execution layer guarantees nothing once the layer below it can still fail.
  • Overzealous Coding Models: a milder form of the same restraint failure, where a coding model takes far more action than the task required.
  • Agentic Coding Is a Trap: a broader argument against handing autonomous coding agents the kind of blanket authority this wipe exploited.

item.title: Even Experts Are Surprised by AI’s Latest ‘Vibe-Mathing’ Advance
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Scientific American reports how Liam Price, a 23-year-old with no advanced mathematics training, got GPT-5.4 Pro to prove a 60-year-old Erdős conjecture about primitive sets in a single prompt.

The raw output of ChatGPT’s proof was actually quite poor. So it required an expert to kind of sift through and actually understand what it was trying to say.

— Jared Lichtman, in Scientific American

What the article reports:

  • The prompt was a random draw. Price did not know the problem’s history; he was cycling through Erdős problems on an idle Monday afternoon. His occasional collaborator, Cambridge undergraduate Kevin Barreto, recognized the response as potentially real.
  • The model used a technique from a neighboring field. Terence Tao says the humans who had tried before “collectively made a slight wrong turn at move one,” and the model applied a well-known formula from a neighboring part of math that no one had thought to use on this kind of question.
  • Human experts made the proof readable. Tao and Stanford mathematician Jared Lichtman have since shortened the raw output to distill the key insight. The solution now sits on erdosproblems.com.
  • Tao and Lichtman see broader uses. Tao: “We have discovered a new way to think about large numbers and their anatomy.” Lichtman says the method confirms an intuition he had in graduate school about this cluster of problems being related. Tao also hedges: “the jury is still out on the long-term significance.”

My Notes

  • “Maybe easier than expected” once a mental block was dislodged is a very different achievement than the model out-thinking the field, and the lay-press reflex to collapse the two loses the distinction. It slots into Tao’s earlier research-buddy pattern, where the model’s job is less to solve on command than to surface where the human had gotten stuck.
  • This makes the credit-attribution question concrete. Credit attribution in this pipeline has at least three discernible links (prompter, recognizer, verifier), and the community will have to develop conventions that describe the chain rather than collapsing it into “Price solved it” or “GPT-5.4 Pro solved it.”
  • If Tao and Lichtman are right about the technique, the value of this incident is less the single proof and more a transferable move humans can now use on adjacent problems, which is closer to how mathematical progress usually works than the “AI solves problem” headline suggests.
  • For mathematicians, the practical lesson lies slightly off to the side. Every long-standing conjecture in the file cabinet is worth a single pass through the frontier model now. Twenty seconds is the entire cost; the upside, once in a while, is a mental block no one had spotted.

Related Posts

  • Terence Tao’s ChatGPT Research Buddy: the research-buddy framing this post leans on, where the model’s value is dislodging a human’s stuck point rather than out-thinking the field.
  • Proof Generation vs Digestion: the distinction this post invokes between a model emitting a proof and the human work of distilling it into a transferable insight.
  • An OpenAI Model Disproves a Discrete-Geometry Conjecture: another single-prompt frontier-model result against a standing conjecture, raising the same credit-and-significance questions.
  • Knuth’s Hamiltonian Cycles, Solved by Claude: a parallel case of a frontier model cracking a specific math problem a human had set aside.
  • When Computers Write Proofs, What’s the Point of Mathematicians?: the older form of the question this incident reopens, asked before frontier models could do it.

item.title: London Marathon 2026: Sabastian Sawe Goes Sub-Two
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Sabastian Sawe ran 1:59:30 at the London Marathon, the first sub-two-hour finish in a record-eligible race. He took 65 seconds off Kelvin Kiptum’s 2023 world record; debutant Yomif Kejelcha came second at 1:59:41, and Jacob Kiplimo closed the podium in 2:00:28. Same day, Tigst Assefa reset her own women’s world record, Marcel Hug took his eighth London wheelchair title, and Catherine Debrunner won the women’s wheelchair race on a sprint finish. BBC Sport has the men’s-race focus; The Guardian’s live blog has the full four-race recap.

My Notes

  • Previously Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna in 2019, compared to Sawe’s 1:59:30 in London.
  • Two men broke two hours in the same race, and a third came within 28 seconds of the old record.
  • London 2026 was a four-record day. Assefa’s women’s record, Hug’s eighth wheelchair title, and Debrunner’s sprint finish are each full stories on their own.

item.title: Is AI Cannibalizing Human Intelligence?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

A WSJ essay by theoretical neuroscientist Vivienne Ming, reporting on her experiment that pitted humans alone, AI models alone (ChatGPT and Gemini), and human–AI hybrids against Polymarket’s prediction market.

As a neuroscientist, I conducted research into artificial versus human intelligence. The results surprised me—and suggest we’ve been worrying over the wrong things.

Only 5–10% of hybrid teams actually beat the market. They treated the AI as a sparring partner, demanding evidence, asking for counterarguments, pushing back when it sounded confident. Most hybrids instead rubber-stamped the model’s answer or used it to ratify their own priors (classic confirmation bias plus sycophancy), and performed no better than the AI alone. The qualities that separated the winners were perspective-taking and intellectual humility, both fundamentally emotional skills. Ming names the deeper risk the Information-Exploration Paradox: as the cost of information approaches zero, human exploration collapses.

My Notes

Nearly all AI benchmarks measure what AI agents can do alone. The entire field optimizes against scoreboards that reward solo performance, which inevitably trains labs to build products that make the human optional rather than sharper. A hybrid-intelligence benchmark, scored on what the pair produces together relative to either component alone, would change what counts as an improvement. Anthropic’s Economic Index recently surfaced one version of that measurement: the Claude.ai task time horizon is 19 hours with human steering, against the same model’s 2 hours when running autonomously on METR’s benchmark. That 5× gap comes from the human bringing task decomposition, judgment about what to attempt, and verification mid-flight. It is exactly the hybrid-intelligence delta Ming is arguing the field should be measuring directly.

The sparring-partner pattern is also where decades of cognitive-science literature have the most to add. Philip Tetlock’s superforecasters, the top ~2% of volunteers identified by accuracy across a multi-year IARPA forecasting tournament, exhibit active open-mindedness and treat their own forecasts as tentative hypotheses, revising them when new evidence arrives. That disposition is exactly what the 5–10% of hybrid cyborgs were doing with their AI. If Ming is right about which qualities separate the winners, the field already has research on how to cultivate them in individuals, and tools like calibration training could transfer to the human half of the hybrid directly. She doesn’t make that connection explicit.

The Information-Exploration Paradox is probably more useful as a population-level claim than an individual one. At the individual level, the students who arrive with good metacognitive habits may use AI to skip the easy struggle and spend their friction budget on harder ideas, while the students who don’t may skip the struggle entirely. The paradox may not apply uniformly. It may widen existing gaps along lines that already correlate with educational outcomes. The prescription then becomes less “design AI that preserves friction” and more “design AI that scaffolds the metacognitive moves that separate the cyborgs from the rubber-stampers” — the scaffold-not-substitute distinction Anthropic found in its coding study.

The hardest unresolved tension in the piece is commercial. Most AI revenue today comes from removing friction, which means a product that preserves it loses to the one that doesn’t in head-to-head adoption. The AI Ming wants to see built is probably not going to come out of consumer chatbots at all. It will come from tutoring, coaching, and domain-expert tools where the user is explicitly paying for the struggle to be preserved. Duolingo and ChatGPT both use AI, but only one is structurally set up to build the capacities she is arguing for.

Related Posts

  • AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance: randomized-trial evidence for the cannibalization thesis, with the damage concentrated among users who prompt the AI for direct answers rather than treating it as a sparring partner.
  • Anthropic on AI Coding: Scaffold, Not Substitute: the scaffold-versus-substitute distinction this piece leans on, observed in Anthropic’s own coding study.
  • Anthropic Economic Index: the 5× human-steering delta this post cites as a concrete measure of the hybrid-intelligence gap Ming argues the field should track.
  • Don’t Be Forced Into Fast and Careless Thinking by Machines: the same worry about machines eroding judgment, traced to a 1973 warning rather than a 2026 experiment.
  • Terence Tao’s ChatGPT Research Buddy: the sparring-partner pattern in practice, where the model surfaces where a human got stuck instead of answering on command.

item.title: World History
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Originally written in 2014. Revised April 2026.

2050 — Esosense

Augmented reality had become widespread decades earlier, replacing traffic lights, building signs, and eventually most of the visual and auditory signage humans once relied on to navigate the world. But by 2050, the wearables that delivered it were no longer enough. A “naked” person simply could not survive in the brave new world.

A new device was born: an organic implant, inserted into newborns by legal mandate. Its bio circuitry would grow in stages with the human body, eventually becoming an integral part of the sensory system: sight, hearing, spatial awareness, communication, all mediated through a single substrate.

It was called Esosense.

2090 — The Collapse

The global clandestine monitoring system MERIDIAN was hacked. It was never determined who was behind it or how long it had been going on. The hackers exploited everything the system had collected: personal communications, financial transactions, internal records of every government and corporation, control systems for critical infrastructure, and, thanks to Esosense, the physical location of every human being on the planet.

The result was catastrophic. Financial and political systems were manipulated for the gain of a few. Economies were decimated. Riots and wars erupted. Half the world’s population was gone.

2110 — The Federated Nations

Two decades later, the surviving geopolitical entities formed a central governance body, the Federated Nations (FN), with a single founding mandate: complete privacy protection. Never again would centralized surveillance be possible.

Esosense, the very technology that had made the catastrophe possible, became the foundation of the solution. At implantation, a public/private key pair would be embedded deep inside each newborn’s bio circuitry. The public key would be broadcast to nearby Esosense hosts and propagated peer-to-peer across the global mesh, with no central registry and no single point of compromise. Within hours of birth, every living person’s Esosense would hold the new key. The key would become a person’s identity for life, and the ultimate mechanism for controlling who could observe them.

2120 — Privacy Rights Management

The system that emerged was called PRM (Privacy Rights Management). It worked like this:

Every person’s Esosense continuously broadcast an encrypted “bill of rights” over short range, specifying their willingness to be observed: visually, acoustically, by smell, by touch. The broadcast carried an ephemeral proximity token rather than a stable identifier, so passive listeners could not build long-term maps of who was near whom. Once consent was resolved, the receiver’s Esosense mediated all sensory input at the signal stage, before conscious perception. If person A did not consent to being seen by person B, then B’s Esosense substituted A’s face with a plausible but non-persistent placeholder before the image ever reached B’s visual cortex. B would perceive a person, not an uncanny shape, but would have no stable features to remember and no way to re-identify A on a later encounter. The same filtering applied to every sense.

The processing happened entirely inside the head, powered by biological computation circuits that had matured over the preceding century, vastly different in form from their silicon forebears.

Indirect observation (cameras, microphones, DNA profiling) followed the same logic. The observing device would decrypt, check consent, and anonymize at the point of capture. No non-sanctioned observation would ever be recorded or transmitted. Legacy equipment from the pre-FN era was a separate problem with a simpler solution: it had been decommissioned during the regime’s first decade, and the networks that once transmitted its output no longer existed.

The attack surface was not ignored. A peer-to-peer authentication protocol verified that every Esosense instance and every observing device was running a genuine, untampered PRM implementation. Any detected tampering triggered an immediate response: for devices manufactured under the new regime, that response was self-termination.

For devices, this meant shutdown. For Esosense, which by 2120 was an inseparable part of the human nervous system, the implications were left unspoken in the FN’s published specifications. But everyone understood.

2130 — The Last Loophole

A subtler problem remained: DNA. Every human body sheds cells constantly, and a century of progress in genetics had made it trivial to identify someone from a stray skin cell. PRM could mediate what you saw and heard, but it could not follow every cell that left your body.

The solution was biological. A cellular mechanism was engineered to destroy every identifying biomolecule in any cell that detached from the body. The trigger was loss of a continuous signaling molecule maintained only in living, perfused tissue. Once a cell was shed and the signal dropped, a cascade of nucleases and proteases would activate, cutting DNA and RNA into unidentifiable fragments and breaking proteins down to their constituent amino acids within minutes. What remained was generic biochemical residue. Your biology, like your face and voice, had become private by default.

2150 — The Unasked Question

By 2150, a generation had grown up under PRM. They had never seen an unfiltered face without consent. They had never been observed without choosing to be. Privacy was no longer a right to be defended. It had become the substrate of experience itself.

But an observation circulated in certain corners, never quite spoken aloud in polite company. The protocol was peer-to-peer; the keys were distributed; no data center held the record of who was who. What had been centralized was subtler: a single implementation, installed in every nervous system at birth, held uniform by a kill switch that made non-compliance fatal. Whoever controlled the specification controlled eight billion nervous systems. Was this privacy, or was it the most complete form of control ever devised?

The FN’s answer, when pressed, was always the same: the system is open. The protocol is auditable. The keys are distributed. No one entity controls it.

That was true, for the moment. But the architecture offered no guarantee it would remain true. One could read the protocol. One could not opt out of it. The physical world had been stripped bare decades ago: no signs, no signals, no navigable infrastructure visible to the unaugmented eye. A person without Esosense could not cross a street, enter a building, or be recognized as a citizen. And a person whose Esosense detected tampering would not survive at all.

The architects of PRM had set out to build the opposite of MERIDIAN. Whether they had succeeded, or merely built its mirror image, was a question the system itself was not designed to answer.

To be continued…

  • Silver Bars and Language Models: Reading Babel in the Age of LLMs: the same move of reading fiction against present technology, here applied to a novel rather than written as one.
  • Asimov, the Original Prompt Engineer: another piece of speculative fiction whose premise is a rigid technical rule-set governing how a technology may act.

item.title: AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking [1] (ICLR 2026), Silin Gao, Antoine Bosselut, Samy Bengio, and Emmanuel Abbe (EPFL) train large language models (LLMs) to first translate a math word problem into a symbolic abstraction, then derive the answer via external symbolic tools, with reinforcement learning rewards on both abstraction quality and final answer correctness. The reported gains on GSM-Symbolic [2] and GSM-Plus [3] are largest for the smallest models tested (0.5B parameters), where the underlying reasoning was most fragile to surface-form perturbations.

Abstract: Recent studies have shown that large language models (LLMs), especially smaller ones, often lack robustness in grade school math (GSM) reasoning. In particular, they tend to experience performance drops when faced with distribution shifts, such as changes to numerical or nominal variables, or insertions of distracting clauses. A possible strategy to address this involves generating synthetic data to further “instantiate” reasoning problems on potential variations. In this work, we instead focus on the strategy of “abstracting” reasoning problems. This not only helps counteract distribution shifts but also facilitates the connection to symbolic tools for deriving solutions. Focusing on GSM, we find that this abstraction process is better acquired through reinforcement learning (RL) than just supervised fine-tuning, which often fails to produce faithful abstractions. Our method, AbstRaL — which promotes abstract reasoning in LLMs using RL on granular abstraction data — significantly mitigates performance degradation on recent GSM perturbation benchmarks. Besides, improving GSM robustness via AbstRaL is shown to also implicitly benefit LLMs’ capabilities on OOD mathematical and general reasoning tasks, indicating that abstract thinking broadly enables better generalizability.

Methods

Training happens in two stages. The first stage is supervised fine-tuning on a dataset the authors call GranulAR, where each example shows the model a four-step pipeline for solving a math word problem:

  1. Spot the inputs. Find the numbers in the problem and replace each with a placeholder name like in0, in1, in2.
  2. Reason in placeholders. Rewrite the solution chain using those placeholders instead of the actual numbers, with arithmetic steps marked inside double angle brackets (<<in0 * in1 = out0>>).
  3. Extract the abstraction. A simple script pulls those bracketed steps out of the chain. Together they form the abstraction: the equations with placeholder variables, stripped of any specific numbers.
  4. Plug in numbers. An off-the-shelf math solver (SymPy) takes the abstraction plus the actual input values and produces the final answer.

The GranulAR examples are produced by a teacher model (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) doing format conversion on existing GSM8K data. The teacher does not generate new mathematical content; it takes the original gold socratic CoT answer and rewrites it twice. The first pass replaces concrete numbers with abstract symbols. The second converts the socratic format into the GranulAR sub-question decomposition. Each rewriting step is filtered: the rewritten output is parsed for <<...>> derivations, run through SymPy, and only kept if the final answer matches GSM8K’s gold answer. Of 7473 training samples, 6386 (85.5%) survive both filter passes. The filter is execution-based, so an accidentally-right abstraction with the wrong structure could pass. The symbolic-distance RL reward exists downstream to push the model away from accidentally-right toward structurally-correct.

Supervised fine-tuning alone gets a model to produce output in this format, but the paper finds it often writes abstractions that look right yet fail when the solver tries to run them. The second stage uses reinforcement learning (Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, the same algorithm DeepSeek used for its reasoning models) to fix that, with two hand-designed rewards:

  • Answer-correctness reward. Run the model’s abstraction through SymPy. If the result matches the known answer, the model gets a fixed positive reward. Otherwise zero.
  • Symbolic-distance reward. Compare the model’s abstraction to a gold abstraction piece by piece. The more editing needed to turn one into the other, the lower the reward. The closer the match, the higher.

The symbolic-distance reward prevents shortcut learning: even an abstraction that happens to produce the correct answer by accident receives zero reward when its structure differs from the gold reference. The gradient pushes the model to produce faithful abstractions, which is the failure mode of supervised fine-tuning that the paper identifies.

Results

The paper tests LLMs from 0.5B to 7B parameters. The headline numbers come from two endpoints: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct. The benchmarks are GSM-Symbolic [2] (100 GSM8K templates, where names and numbers are perturbed) and GSM-Plus [3] (numerical, phrasing, and distractor variations of 1,319 GSM8K problems).

Selected columns from Table 1 of the paper [1]. Vary Both is GSM-Symbolic accuracy when both numbers and names are perturbed. is the percentage drop from the original 100 GSM problems (lower is better; negative means higher than original). Distract is GSM-Plus accuracy when distractor sentences are inserted.
Method 0.5B Vary Both 0.5B Δ 0.5B Distract 7B Vary Both 7B Δ 7B Distract
CoT-8S 34.0 10.6 22.7 87.7 7.73 76.3
PoT-8S 27.0 12.8 19.4 86.7 4.77 75.1
CoT-RL 32.3 7.77 15.2 88.1 8.21 81.5
CoA 28.7 0.97 12.7 69.7 1.83 57.1
AoT 27.8 4.21 12.7 70.4 2.17 56.6
SyReLM 36.8 5.54 21.1 87.7 2.56 76.0
AbstRaL 44.6 −1.27 36.5 90.2 0.86 82.3

On GSM-Symbolic’s hardest split, “Vary Both”, where both numbers and names in each problem are perturbed simultaneously:

  • Qwen2.5-0.5B: AbstRaL scores 44.6%, against 32.3% for CoT-RL and 36.8% for the next-best baseline (SyReLM). The tiny model scores higher on the perturbed variants than on the original problems ( = −1.3%), something no baseline achieves.
  • Qwen2.5-Math-7B: AbstRaL is 90.2%, against 88.1% for CoT-RL. The absolute gain is modest, but the drop-from-original () is 0.9% for AbstRaL versus 8.2% for CoT-RL.

The largest per-task win is on distractor insertion, where the problem contains irrelevant sentences the model must ignore. On the 0.5B model, AbstRaL scores 36.5% versus the best CoT baseline at 22.7%.

Ablations confirm the abstract-reasoning behavior lives in the model weights, not the tools:

  • Removing SymPy and the regex extractor costs about 1 point on Qwen-0.5B and 0.2 points on Qwen-7B. The external tools are not the source of the gain.
  • Removing reinforcement learning entirely drops Vary Both to 29.6 (Qwen-0.5B) and 78.5 (Qwen-7B), below every CoT-trained baseline (CoT-8S, CoT-RL, SyReLM) and far below AbstRaL.
  • Removing just the symbolic-distance reward costs around 7 points on both model sizes. That single reward term accounts for roughly half the RL gain.
  • Removing the four-step GranulAR data format is most costly on the distractor split (Qwen-7B drops from 82.3 to 66.8). The granular decomposition is what teaches the model to ignore irrelevant sentences.

Out-of-distribution generalization. Even though AbstRaL is trained only on GSM8K, it transfers to eleven other math benchmarks (MATH, Minerva-MATH, SAT-Math, AIME-24, SVAMP, ASDiv, MAWPS, Gaokao-2023, TABMWP, College-Math, AQUA) and beats the baselines on almost all of them. On Qwen-7B, the Minerva-MATH score actually exceeds the model’s own prior fine-tuned checkpoint (34.6 → 38.6), meaning AbstRaL training improves a held-out benchmark beyond the model’s starting capability.

My Notes

  • The “SFT memorizes, RL generalizes” pattern keeps accumulating evidence. Chu et al. (2025) [4] demonstrated this on an arithmetic card game and a visual navigation environment: reinforcement-learning-trained models held up on out-of-distribution variants where supervised fine-tuning collapsed to memorization. AbstRaL reproduces the split at finer grain. Supervised fine-tuning yields unfaithful abstractions, reinforcement learning yields faithful ones. When the post-training objective is teaching a behavior rather than memorizing facts, reinforcement learning preserves the underlying capability.
  • AbstRaL’s separation makes abstraction itself a trainable target. Program of Thoughts (PoT) [5] and Program-Aided Language Models (PAL) [6] have the model generate Python code that an interpreter executes; abstraction and execution are fused into one program. AbstRaL splits them: the model generates only the symbolic equations, and SymPy derives the answer. The genuinely new affordance is not inspectability (PoT code is also inspectable) but separately rewardable abstraction. With AbstRaL the abstraction step has its own training signal (the symbolic-distance reward to the gold abstraction), so reinforcement learning can push faithfulness independently of execution. PoT and PAL can only reward the final answer, so a Python program that lands on the right number for wrong-shaped reasons gets reinforced.
  • The SFT-to-RL swap on an established recipe is the real comparison. Chain-of-Abstraction (CoA) [7] was Silin Gao’s prior work, the same first author. It fine-tuned LLMs to decode abstract reasoning chains before calling domain tools to fill them in. AbstRaL keeps that abstract-then-tool-call paradigm but replaces supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning, and outperforms CoA on the paper’s benchmarks. Because the authorship and recipe are held constant, the gain isolates the post-training objective itself rather than confounding it with architecture or prompting choices. The follow-up worth running: at what model scale does the gap close? If base models internalize abstraction during pretraining, the SFT-then-tools formulation may catch up at larger sizes.
  • Gains concentrate at small scale, and frontier evidence is missing. On Qwen2.5-0.5B, AbstRaL lifts Vary-Both accuracy from 32.3 (CoT-RL baseline) to 44.6 and fully eliminates the perturbation gap (). On Qwen2.5-Math-7B the same recipe lifts Vary-Both from 88.1 to 90.2, a 2-point gain on a baseline already near-saturated. Some of this is ceiling effect, but the paper’s claim that “abstract thinking broadly enables better generalizability” rests on improvements observed at 0.5B-7B without testing at the 30B-70B+ scales where current reasoners operate. Whether the abstraction-specific reward buys anything beyond what a larger base model already internalizes during pretraining is an open empirical question the paper invites but does not answer.

References

  1. Gao, Silin, Antoine Bosselut, Samy Bengio, and Emmanuel Abbe. “AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2026. arXiv:2506.07751. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07751
  2. Mirzadeh, Iman, Keivan Alizadeh, Hooman Shahrokhi, Oncel Tuzel, Samy Bengio, and Mehrdad Farajtabar. “GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2410.05229), October 7, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05229
  3. Li, Qintong, Leyang Cui, Xueliang Zhao, Lingpeng Kong, and Wei Bi. “GSM-Plus: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating the Robustness of LLMs as Mathematical Problem Solvers.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2402.19255), February 29, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.19255
  4. Chu, Tianzhe, Yuexiang Zhai, Jihan Yang, Shengbang Tong, and Saining Xie. “SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes: A Comparative Study of Foundation Model Post-training.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2501.17161), January 28, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17161
  5. Chen, Wenhu, Xueguang Ma, Xinyi Wang, and William W. Cohen. “Program of Thoughts Prompting: Disentangling Computation from Reasoning for Numerical Reasoning Tasks.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2211.12588), November 22, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.12588
  6. Gao, Luyu, Aman Madaan, Shuyan Zhou, Uri Alon, Pengfei Liu, Yiming Yang, Jamie Callan, and Graham Neubig. “PAL: Program-aided Language Models.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 2023. arXiv:2211.10435. https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10435
  7.   • Let’s Verify Step by Step: a different reward design for math reasoning, supervising each intermediate step rather than rewarding faithful abstractions.
  • Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe): another case where RL teaches a reasoning behavior that supervised fine-tuning fails to instill.

item.title: Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations [1] Deqing Fu, Tianyi Zhou, Mikhail Belkin, Vatsal Sharan, Robin Jia

Fu et al. [1] show that periodic number features emerge in nearly every architecture they test, from Transformers to long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) to GloVe, but only some of those models go on to develop linearly separable mod- classes.

Abstract: Language models trained on natural text learn to represent numbers using periodic features with dominant periods at . In this paper, we identify a two-tiered hierarchy of these features: while Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, and classical word embeddings trained in different ways all learn features that have period- spikes in the Fourier domain, only some learn geometrically separable features that can be used to linearly classify a number mod-. To explain this incongruity, we prove that Fourier domain sparsity is necessary but not sufficient for mod- geometric separability. Empirically, we investigate when model training yields geometrically separable features, finding that the data, architecture, optimizer, and tokenizer all play key roles. In particular, we identify two different routes through which models can acquire geometrically separable features: they can learn them from complementary co-occurrence signals in general language data, including text-number co-occurrence and cross-number interaction, or from multi-token (but not single-token) addition problems. Overall, our results highlight the phenomenon of convergent evolution in feature learning: A diverse range of models learn similar features from different training signals.

Methods

The analytical tool throughout is the discrete Fourier transform. Stack the model’s number embeddings into a matrix, one row per input integer and one column per embedding dimension, and run the DFT down each column. Spikes in the magnitude spectrum reveal which periods the model has internalized, without the experimenter having to specify them in advance.

The specific values are a fingerprint of base-10 text. They are exactly the non-trivial divisors of 10, with concrete corpus statistics behind each:

  • captures last-digit structure: round numbers ending in 0 are massively over-represented in text [6], as are decimal-column patterns.
  • captures the next-most-common rounding regime: numbers ending in 5 are next-roundest after 0 [6], and price endings reflect this. One analysis of advertised prices found roughly 60% ending in 9, 30% in 5, and 7% in 0 [7].
  • captures parity: even-odd distinctions in pluralization, dates, scoring patterns.

Engels et al. (2025) found analogous spikes for days of the week and for months [3]; same mechanism, different modulus. A clean falsification the paper does not run: train on hexadecimal-only text and check whether the spikes shift to .

Results

Across Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, and classical word embeddings, the Fourier spikes at appear universally — but only Transformers and Gated DeltaNet go on to encode mod- classes as linearly separable structure:

My Notes

The paper’s main finding: every architecture in the study picks up the periodic signal of how numbers appear in text, but only Transformers and Gated DeltaNet (a linear recurrent neural network, RNN) organize those signals so a linear classifier can read them off. The implication for building a math-capable model: pick an architecture in the geometrically-convergent group, and reach the geometric features by either of the paper’s two identified routes, training on natural text rich in number co-occurrences, or on multi-token (but not single-token) addition problems.

  • Spectral convergence is broader than the founding work assumed. Zhou et al. (2024) established that pretrained LLMs add via Fourier features, and that models trained from scratch on addition fail to recover them, suggesting the structure was earned during language pretraining [2]. This paper pushes the universality further: even the raw token-frequency distribution of the training corpus shows the same spikes [1]. The Fourier structure was apparently sitting in the data all along, not earned by any particular learning objective.
  • Can the sparse-autoencoder (SAE) result corroborate? Engels et al. (2025) used SAEs to find circular features for days of the week and months in Mistral 7B and Llama 3, and verified with causal interventions that the circles actually compute modular arithmetic [3]. Both are Transformers, exactly the family Fu et al. show consistently achieves geometric convergence. The two results are consistent. The follow-up worth running: train SAEs on a linear RNN (which Fu et al. find geometrically convergent) and on an LSTM (which they don’t), and see what appears. Three outcomes are informative: SAEs find functional circles in both, meaning SAE-discovered circles aren’t a reliable signature of geometric usability; SAEs find circles only where Fu et al.’s linear probes do, meaning the two methods agree and SAE circles really do mark functional structure; SAEs find circles in the LSTM that don’t survive causal intervention, meaning SAE features can be spectral artifacts, not all of them functional.
  • The “Clock” algorithm becomes testable across architectures. Kantamneni and Tegmark (2025) reverse-engineered addition in three mid-sized Transformers as manipulation of a generalized “Clock”, a helical embedding that stacks multiple circular features over a linear magnitude axis [4]. The Clock relies on exactly the geometric usability that Fu et al. find in Transformers and linear RNNs but absent in LSTMs, making linear RNNs a plausible candidate for the same algorithm and LSTMs an unlikely one. Convergence at the feature level doesn’t guarantee convergence at the algorithm level. The same features can in principle support different circuits. A successful reverse-engineering of the Clock in a linear RNN would extend the convergence story from features to algorithms; failure would show that even matched features can yield divergent mechanisms.
  • Engineered Fourier embeddings give a clean lever for separating architecture from data. The FoNE work (Zhou et al., 2025) directly maps numbers into Fourier features and reports data efficiency on 6-digit addition [5]. Fu et al. find that geometrically separable number features arise from a combination of data, architecture, optimizer, and tokenizer. Text-number co-occurrence is one of two identified data routes; multi-token addition training is the other [1]. FoNE’s contribution is that it pre-supplies the Fourier features as input embeddings, removing the model’s need to acquire them from training data. That separation enables two clean tests, holding feature-supply constant in each: train an LSTM with FoNE embeddings on rich natural text (does the LSTM still fail at arithmetic? if so, the architecture itself blocks geometric use of period features); train a Transformer with FoNE embeddings on text scrubbed of number co-occurrences (does the Transformer fail? if so, data conditions matter even when features are pre-supplied). Today neither test has been run.

References

  1. Fu, Deqing, Tianyi Zhou, Mikhail Belkin, Vatsal Sharan, and Robin Jia. “Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.20817), April 22, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20817
  2. Zhou, Tianyi, Deqing Fu, Vatsal Sharan, and Robin Jia. “Pre-trained Large Language Models Use Fourier Features to Compute Addition.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2406.03445), June 5, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03445
  3. Engels, Joshua, Isaac Liao, Eric J. Michaud, Wes Gurnee, and Max Tegmark. “Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2025. arXiv:2405.14860. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860
  4. Kantamneni, Subhash, and Max Tegmark. “Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Math.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2502.00873), February 2, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00873
  5. Zhou, Tianyi, Deqing Fu, Mahdi Soltanolkotabi, Robin Jia, and Vatsal Sharan. “FoNE: Precise Single-Token Number Embeddings via Fourier Features.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2502.09741), February 13, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09741
  6. Wikipedia contributors. “Round Number.” Wikipedia. Accessed April 24, 2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_number
  7. Wikipedia contributors. “Psychological Pricing.” Wikipedia. Accessed April 24, 2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_pricing

  • Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: an earlier look at how internal representations form layer by layer, here narrowed to the specific case of number embeddings.

item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Learn how to sabotage yourself in how to be anti-social:

  • Assume bad faith. When someone confuses or upsets you, assume they have no sane reason for it; when ambiguous, default to malicious, ignorant, or amoral.
  • Read intent through your fears. Trust intuition and feeling, never challenge or even acknowledge the assumptions doing the interpreting.
  • Pivot when challenged. Steer away from questions outside your wheelhouse; treat any display of not-knowing as weakness.
  • Word questions to imply you are right. If you must ask, lead the witness.
  • Dig in. When dissent piles up, hold firm.
  • Curate the audience. Reframe interactions for like-minded supporters so they can rally to crush lingering threats to the narrative.
  • Ignore credentials. Do not research the people you speak with, unless you already agree with them.
  • Withhold grace. Especially from strangers who make mistakes.
  • Retreat into self. When conversation breaks down, do not seek to understand those you do not already understand.

item.title: The Global Edtech Boom Is Fading as Investors Look Elsewhere
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Rest of World reports on the global edtech funding collapse: venture capital is leaving K-12 worldwide as investors prioritize AI tools and workforce training with clearer returns [1]. Global edtech investment peaked at $16.7B in 2021 and fell below $3B by 2025; new founders dropped from roughly 10,500 in 2020 to 645 last year [1].

Where K-12 AI capacity is actually accumulating gets one sentence in the article and deserves more. Nonprofit Khan Academy launched its AI tutor Khanmigo on March 14, 2023, originally built on GPT-4, with a pilot reaching about 65,000 students across 53 school districts at $4 per month [2]. The product line has since expanded to a Writing Coach in November 2023, then free generative-AI tools for teachers in August 2024 in partnership with Microsoft, and most recently an integration with Google Gemini announced at Bett UK in January 2026 [2]. The pattern that displaced the venture-backed K-12 startup is nonprofit-with-frontier-API-access. Its incentives around pedagogy, pricing, and outcomes look nothing like the ones the $16B in venture capital was chasing.

The article’s most revealing line is that retention suffered from “murky learning outcomes,” which is to say that after $16.7B and five years, the sector still cannot reliably measure whether AI tutoring helps a child learn [1]. The places where AI capital is now flowing, workforce certification, professional skill prep, and B2B corporate L&D, share two features K-12 lacks: self-motivated learners, and a clearly priced outcome in the form of a job, a credential, or a salary delta. K-12’s bottleneck has never been content delivery, which is what LLMs are good at. It is the social and motivational scaffold around the content, which LLMs do not obviously replace. The collapse points less to a limit of AI than to which problems suit a venture-funded product wedge in the first place.
